    Bayesian fitting of QENS data: from the posterior to derived quantities¶

    A least-squares fit reports one best value and one symmetric uncertainty for each parameter. A Bayesian analysis reports the whole posterior distribution: how probable each combination of parameter values is, given the data. This notebook samples the posterior of a QENS model with the DREAM algorithm, and then compares two ways of getting the uncertainty of a quantity that is derived from the parameters: the first-order propagation of es.math, and the posterior itself.

    The model and the data are those of the notebook on fitting QENS data with a Lorentzian, which is the better place to start. Each part here closes with a few exercises on what was just shown. Their hints and solutions are folded away and open on a click, so the text reads straight through; a solution is a worked answer with its result.

    Copied!

    The data and the model¶

    The data are simulated and reduced QENS intensities, as in the notebook on fitting QENS data, for the energy transfer $\omega$ in meV, cropped to $|\omega| < 0.06$ meV:

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    filename = pooch.retrieve(
    url='https://public.esss.dk/groups/scipp/dmsc-summer-school/2025/4-reduction/energy_transfer_QENS_unknown_quasi_elastic_many_neutrons.dat',
    known_hash='sha256:e49fa9a1d2ef5eeb714524903e8ffa9de6616e5a299a799cbb0b2f3ee8fd459a',
)
omega, intensity, error = np.loadtxt(filename, unpack=True)
keep = np.isfinite(intensity) & (omega > -0.06) & (omega < 0.06)
omega, intensity, error = omega[keep], intensity[keep], error[keep]

print(f'{omega.size} points')

    Downloading data from 'https://public.esss.dk/groups/scipp/dmsc-summer-school/2025/4-reduction/energy_transfer_QENS_unknown_quasi_elastic_many_neutrons.dat' to file '/home/runner/.cache/pooch/13c45bd8472df2cbc0ff550e2ec9ed15-energy_transfer_QENS_unknown_quasi_elastic_many_neutrons.dat'.

    120 points

    The model is a Lorentzian with area $A$, half width $\gamma$ and centre $\omega_0$, convolved with a Gaussian resolution of width $\sigma$. The min and max of every parameter are not only the range of a fit: for the sampler they define a uniform prior, so the sampler only visits values inside the range.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    class Quasielastic(ModelBase):
    """A Lorentzian convolved with a Gaussian resolution, as a function of the energy transfer."""

    def __init__(self, area: float, gamma: float, omega_0: float, sigma: float):
        super().__init__()
        self._area = Parameter(name='area', value=area, min=0.01, max=100)
        self._gamma = Parameter(name='gamma', value=gamma, unit='meV', min=1e-4, max=1e-2)
        self._omega_0 = Parameter(name='omega_0', value=omega_0, unit='meV', min=0, max=2e-3)
        self._sigma = Parameter(name='sigma', value=sigma, unit='meV', min=1e-5, max=1e-1)

    @property
    def area(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._area

    @property
    def gamma(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._gamma

    @property
    def omega_0(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._omega_0

    @property
    def sigma(self) -> Parameter:
        return self._sigma

    def __call__(self, omega):
        width = self._gamma.value
        lorentzian = (
            self._area.value / np.pi * width / ((omega - self._omega_0.value) ** 2 + width**2)
        )
        resolution = norm(0, self._sigma.value).pdf(omega)
        resolution /= resolution.sum()
        return np.convolve(lorentzian, resolution, 'same')
    class Quasielastic(ModelBase): """A Lorentzian convolved with a Gaussian resolution, as a function of the energy transfer.""" def __init__(self, area: float, gamma: float, omega_0: float, sigma: float): super().__init__() self._area = Parameter(name='area', value=area, min=0.01, max=100) self._gamma = Parameter(name='gamma', value=gamma, unit='meV', min=1e-4, max=1e-2) self._omega_0 = Parameter(name='omega_0', value=omega_0, unit='meV', min=0, max=2e-3) self._sigma = Parameter(name='sigma', value=sigma, unit='meV', min=1e-5, max=1e-1) @property def area(self) -> Parameter: return self._area @property def gamma(self) -> Parameter: return self._gamma @property def omega_0(self) -> Parameter: return self._omega_0 @property def sigma(self) -> Parameter: return self._sigma def __call__(self, omega): width = self._gamma.value lorentzian = ( self._area.value / np.pi * width / ((omega - self._omega_0.value) ** 2 + width**2) ) resolution = norm(0, self._sigma.value).pdf(omega) resolution /= resolution.sum() return np.convolve(lorentzian, resolution, 'same')

    Start from a fit¶

    The sampler starts its chains close to the current parameter values, so it is worth fitting first. The fit also gives the reference for the comparison below: a value and a first-order uncertainty for every parameter. The sampler moves the parameters while it works, so the fitted numbers are kept in separate DescriptorNumbers:

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    model = Quasielastic(area=10.0, gamma=8e-3, omega_0=1e-3, sigma=1e-3)
fitter = Fitter(model, model)
fitter.fit(x=omega, y=intensity, weights=1 / error)

fitted = {
    parameter.name: DescriptorNumber(
        name=parameter.name,
        value=parameter.value,
        unit=parameter.unit,
        variance=parameter.variance,
    )
    for parameter in (model.area, model.gamma, model.omega_0, model.sigma)
}
for name, number in fitted.items():
    show(name, number)
    model = Quasielastic(area=10.0, gamma=8e-3, omega_0=1e-3, sigma=1e-3) fitter = Fitter(model, model) fitter.fit(x=omega, y=intensity, weights=1 / error) fitted = { parameter.name: DescriptorNumber( name=parameter.name, value=parameter.value, unit=parameter.unit, variance=parameter.variance, ) for parameter in (model.area, model.gamma, model.omega_0, model.sigma) } for name, number in fitted.items(): show(name, number)
    area = 5.227 ± 0.05 dimensionless
gamma = 0.007161 ± 0.00014 meV
omega_0 = 0.001142 ± 9.4e-05 meV
sigma = 0.001087 ± 0.00059 meV

    Sampling the posterior¶

    DREAM is an ensemble Markov-chain Monte Carlo method: many chains explore the parameter space in parallel and exchange information. The sampler takes the configured fitter, the data and the weights, and returns the draws. The sampler requires a Bumps minimizer, so the fitter is switched to it first. The run takes a few tens of seconds.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    fitter.switch_minimizer(AvailableMinimizers.Bumps)
sampler = Sampler(fitter, omega, intensity, weights=1 / error)
results = sampler.sample(samples=20000, burn=500, thin=2)

columns = {
    parameter.name: results.draws[:, results.param_names.index(parameter.unique_name)]
    for parameter in (model.area, model.gamma, model.omega_0, model.sigma)
}
print(f'{results.draws.shape[0]} draws for {results.draws.shape[1]} parameters')
    fitter.switch_minimizer(AvailableMinimizers.Bumps) sampler = Sampler(fitter, omega, intensity, weights=1 / error) results = sampler.sample(samples=20000, burn=500, thin=2) columns = { parameter.name: results.draws[:, results.param_names.index(parameter.unique_name)] for parameter in (model.area, model.gamma, model.omega_0, model.sigma) } print(f'{results.draws.shape[0]} draws for {results.draws.shape[1]} parameters')
    9600 draws for 4 parameters

    Before the draws are used, the chains have to be checked for convergence. The Gelman-Rubin statistic $\hat{R}$ compares the variation within each chain with the variation between chains. Values close to 1 mean that the chains agree: below 1.1 is acceptable and below 1.01 is strict. If a value is higher, draw more samples:

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    for name, value in zip(results.param_names, results.state.gelman()):
    parameter = next(
        p for p in (model.area, model.gamma, model.omega_0, model.sigma) if p.unique_name == name
    )
    print(f'R-hat of {parameter.name:8s} {value:.3f}')
    for name, value in zip(results.param_names, results.state.gelman()): parameter = next( p for p in (model.area, model.gamma, model.omega_0, model.sigma) if p.unique_name == name ) print(f'R-hat of {parameter.name:8s} {value:.3f}')
    R-hat of area     1.014
R-hat of gamma    1.018
R-hat of omega_0  1.019
R-hat of sigma    1.019

    The median and the interval that holds the central 68 % of the draws summarise each marginal posterior. They can be compared with the fitted value and its symmetric uncertainty:

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    for name, draws in columns.items():
    low, median, high = np.percentile(draws, [16, 50, 84])
    number = fitted[name]
    print(
        f'{name:8s} fit {number.value:.4g} ± {number.error:.2g}   posterior {median:.4g} (+{high - median:.2g} / -{median - low:.2g})'
    )
    for name, draws in columns.items(): low, median, high = np.percentile(draws, [16, 50, 84]) number = fitted[name] print( f'{name:8s} fit {number.value:.4g} ± {number.error:.2g} posterior {median:.4g} (+{high - median:.2g} / -{median - low:.2g})' )
    area     fit 5.227 ± 0.05   posterior 5.225 (+0.053 / -0.053)
gamma    fit 0.007161 ± 0.00014   posterior 0.007148 (+0.00013 / -0.00016)
omega_0  fit 0.001142 ± 9.4e-05   posterior 0.001123 (+0.0001 / -0.00011)
sigma    fit 0.001087 ± 0.00059   posterior 0.001144 (+0.00058 / -0.00053)

    The draws also show how the parameters vary together. The correlation coefficient of two parameters lies between $-1$ and $+1$; a value far from 0 means that the data cannot determine the two independently. The first-order arithmetic of es.math ignores this.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    names = list(columns)
correlation = np.corrcoef([columns[name] for name in names])
for i, first in enumerate(names):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(names)):
        print(f'correlation of {first} and {names[j]}: {correlation[i, j]:+.2f}')
    names = list(columns) correlation = np.corrcoef([columns[name] for name in names]) for i, first in enumerate(names): for j in range(i + 1, len(names)): print(f'correlation of {first} and {names[j]}: {correlation[i, j]:+.2f}')
    correlation of area and gamma: +0.14
correlation of area and omega_0: +0.01
correlation of area and sigma: -0.09
correlation of gamma and omega_0: -0.08
correlation of gamma and sigma: -0.68
correlation of omega_0 and sigma: +0.20

    A derived quantity from the draws¶

    Every draw is a possible set of parameters, so a derived quantity can be computed for every draw. The distribution of the results is the posterior of that quantity, with no approximation. The relaxation time is $\tau = \hbar/\gamma$. On the draws this is plain NumPy, because es.math takes one Parameter at a time. The first-order propagation of es.math starts from the fitted value:

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    hbar = DescriptorNumber(name='hbar', value=0.6582119569, unit='meV*ps', variance=0.0)

tau_first_order = hbar / fitted['gamma']
tau_draws = hbar.value / columns['gamma']
low, median, high = np.percentile(tau_draws, [16, 50, 84])

show('relaxation time, first order', tau_first_order)
print(f'relaxation time, posterior = {median:.4g} (+{high - median:.2g} / -{median - low:.2g}) ps')
    hbar = DescriptorNumber(name='hbar', value=0.6582119569, unit='meV*ps', variance=0.0) tau_first_order = hbar / fitted['gamma'] tau_draws = hbar.value / columns['gamma'] low, median, high = np.percentile(tau_draws, [16, 50, 84]) show('relaxation time, first order', tau_first_order) print(f'relaxation time, posterior = {median:.4g} (+{high - median:.2g} / -{median - low:.2g}) ps')
    relaxation time, first order = 91.92 ± 1.8 ps
relaxation time, posterior = 92.09 (+2.1 / -1.7) ps

    The width $\gamma$ is determined well, so the two agree closely. The chart shows the posterior of $\tau$ with the Gaussian that the first-order uncertainty describes:

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    grid = np.linspace(tau_draws.min(), tau_draws.max(), 300)
gaussian = norm(tau_first_order.value, tau_first_order.error).pdf(grid)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(
    go.Histogram(
        x=tau_draws, histnorm='probability density', nbinsx=60, name='posterior', opacity=0.6
    )
)
fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=grid, y=gaussian, mode='lines', name='first order', line=dict(color='black'))
)
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title='relaxation time / ps',
    yaxis_title='probability density',
    bargap=0.02,
    margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=30, b=50),
    legend=dict(x=0.7, y=0.95),
)
show_figure(fig)
    grid = np.linspace(tau_draws.min(), tau_draws.max(), 300) gaussian = norm(tau_first_order.value, tau_first_order.error).pdf(grid) fig = go.Figure() fig.add_trace( go.Histogram( x=tau_draws, histnorm='probability density', nbinsx=60, name='posterior', opacity=0.6 ) ) fig.add_trace( go.Scatter(x=grid, y=gaussian, mode='lines', name='first order', line=dict(color='black')) ) fig.update_layout( xaxis_title='relaxation time / ps', yaxis_title='probability density', bargap=0.02, margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=30, b=50), legend=dict(x=0.7, y=0.95), ) show_figure(fig)

    Exercise 1: The half-life from the posterior¶

    The intermediate scattering function falls to one half at $t_{1/2} = \tau \ln 2$. Work out $t_{1/2}$ for every draw, print its median and its central 68 % interval, and print the first-order value from the fitted width for comparison.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    hbar = DescriptorNumber(name='hbar', value=0.6582119569, unit='meV*ps', variance=0.0)
two = DescriptorNumber(name='two', value=2.0, variance=0.0)
gamma_draws = columns['gamma']
    hbar = DescriptorNumber(name='hbar', value=0.6582119569, unit='meV*ps', variance=0.0) two = DescriptorNumber(name='two', value=2.0, variance=0.0) gamma_draws = columns['gamma']
    Hint 1

    Compute the half-life for every draw at once with NumPy: es.math takes one number at a time, so it is not used on the draws. np.percentile(..., [16, 50, 84]) gives the median and the central 68 % interval.

    Hint 2

    The half-life is the relaxation time times $\ln 2$, and the relaxation time is $\hbar/\gamma$. For the first-order value use es.math.log on the constant two and the fitted width fitted['gamma'].

    Solution
    t_half_draws = hbar.value / gamma_draws * np.log(2)
low, median, high = np.percentile(t_half_draws, [16, 50, 84])
show('half-life, first order', hbar / fitted['gamma'] * es.math.log(two))
print(f'half-life, posterior = {median:.4g} (+{high - median:.2g} / -{median - low:.2g}) ps')

    Output:

    half-life, first order = 63.71 ± 1.3 ps
half-life, posterior = 63.83 (+1.5 / -1.2) ps

    The two agree closely, because $\gamma$ is well determined and $t_{1/2}$ is nearly linear in it over its range.

    A poorly determined parameter¶

    The resolution width $\sigma$ is known much less well than $\gamma$. A quantity that depends on its inverse, such as the coherence time $\hbar/\sigma$ that belongs to the resolution width, is a strongly non-linear function of it. The first-order uncertainty is symmetric, while the posterior is not:

    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    coherence_first_order = hbar / fitted['sigma']
coherence_draws = hbar.value / columns['sigma']
low, median, high = np.percentile(coherence_draws, [16, 50, 84])

show('coherence time, first order', coherence_first_order)
print(f'coherence time, posterior = {median:.4g} (+{high - median:.2g} / -{median - low:.2g}) ps')
    coherence_first_order = hbar / fitted['sigma'] coherence_draws = hbar.value / columns['sigma'] low, median, high = np.percentile(coherence_draws, [16, 50, 84]) show('coherence time, first order', coherence_first_order) print(f'coherence time, posterior = {median:.4g} (+{high - median:.2g} / -{median - low:.2g}) ps')
    coherence time, first order = 605.3 ± 3.3e+02 ps
coherence time, posterior = 575.3 (+5e+02 / -1.9e+02) ps
    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    limit = np.percentile(coherence_draws, 99)
grid = np.linspace(0.0, limit, 300)
gaussian = norm(coherence_first_order.value, coherence_first_order.error).pdf(grid)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(
    go.Histogram(
        x=coherence_draws[coherence_draws < limit],
        histnorm='probability density',
        nbinsx=60,
        name='posterior',
        opacity=0.6,
    )
)
fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=grid, y=gaussian, mode='lines', name='first order', line=dict(color='black'))
)
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title='coherence time / ps',
    yaxis_title='probability density',
    bargap=0.02,
    margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=30, b=50),
    legend=dict(x=0.7, y=0.95),
)
show_figure(fig)
    limit = np.percentile(coherence_draws, 99) grid = np.linspace(0.0, limit, 300) gaussian = norm(coherence_first_order.value, coherence_first_order.error).pdf(grid) fig = go.Figure() fig.add_trace( go.Histogram( x=coherence_draws[coherence_draws < limit], histnorm='probability density', nbinsx=60, name='posterior', opacity=0.6, ) ) fig.add_trace( go.Scatter(x=grid, y=gaussian, mode='lines', name='first order', line=dict(color='black')) ) fig.update_layout( xaxis_title='coherence time / ps', yaxis_title='probability density', bargap=0.02, margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=30, b=50), legend=dict(x=0.7, y=0.95), ) show_figure(fig)

    The posterior has a long tail towards long times: its central 68 % interval reaches much further above the median than below it. The first-order interval is symmetric and cannot show this.

    Exercise 2: A quantity that is linear¶

    The resolution full width at half maximum, $2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\;\sigma$, is proportional to $\sigma$. Print the standard deviation of its draws, in µeV, and the first-order uncertainty from es.math.

    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    two = DescriptorNumber(name='two', value=2.0, variance=0.0)
sigma_draws = columns['sigma']
    two = DescriptorNumber(name='two', value=2.0, variance=0.0) sigma_draws = columns['sigma']
    Hint 1

    On the draws use NumPy and the factor between $\sigma$ and the full width at half maximum. 1 meV is 1000 µeV.

    Hint 2

    For the first-order value use es.math.sqrt and es.math.log on the constant two and on the fitted width fitted['sigma'], then convert_unit('ueV').

    Solution
    fwhm_draws = 2 * np.sqrt(2 * np.log(2)) * sigma_draws * 1000
fwhm = 2 * es.math.sqrt(2 * es.math.log(two)) * fitted['sigma']
fwhm.convert_unit('ueV')
print(f'standard deviation of the draws = {fwhm_draws.std():.3g} µeV')
show('resolution FWHM, first order', fwhm)

    Output:

    standard deviation of the draws = 1.22 µeV
resolution FWHM, first order = 2.561 ± 1.4 µeV

    For a linear function the two uncertainties are of the same size; the difference above came from the non-linearity.

    Exercise 3: How likely is a coarse resolution?¶

    Count the fraction of the draws in which the resolution full width at half maximum, $2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\;\sigma$, is larger than 3 µeV. Print it as a percentage. This is the posterior probability of the statement.

    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    sigma_draws = columns['sigma']
    sigma_draws = columns['sigma']
    Hint 1

    Compute the draws of the full width at half maximum in µeV as in the previous exercise, and compare them with 3.

    Hint 2

    The mean of a boolean array is the fraction of True values.

    Solution
    fwhm_draws = 2 * np.sqrt(2 * np.log(2)) * sigma_draws * 1000
probability = (fwhm_draws > 3).mean()
print(f'probability that the resolution FWHM exceeds 3 µeV: {probability:.1%}')

    Output:

    probability that the resolution FWHM exceeds 3 µeV: 40.9%

    A posterior answers a question like this directly; a symmetric uncertainty can only suggest it.

    Good to know¶

    • The draws change from run to run. DREAM is a random algorithm, so the numbers differ a little every time the notebook runs. Increasing samples makes them more stable, and the convergence check above says whether they can be trusted.
    • es.math is for fitted values; NumPy is for draws. es.math works on one Parameter at a time and gives a first-order, symmetric uncertainty. For a quantity that is nearly linear in well-determined parameters it is a quick and accurate shortcut. For a strongly non-linear quantity of a poorly determined parameter, compute it on the draws.
    • The sampler moves the parameters. After sampling, model.gamma.value is no longer the fitted value. That is why the fitted numbers were copied to fitted first.
